summary: This report summarizes the POISED working group, covering the events that led to its formation and its work through the end of 1992. POISED looked at how the IETF should organize its own processes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1396 is the report of a working group that looked at how the people running the Internet standards process were chosen and how decisions were made. It explains the argument that triggered the review, the two changes the group agreed on, and the legal questions it left for the Internet Society.

subtitle: How the IETF rewrote the rules for choosing its own leaders in the winter of 1992.

tldr.problem: By 1992 the Internet community was growing faster than its own procedures could keep up with, and a technical argument about the next version of IP turned into a political argument about who had the right to decide.
tldr.mechanism: The POISED working group met by mail and at the November IETF meeting in Washington, and settled two things: that the IESG would make every standards decision, and that the IAB and IESG members would be picked by a committee of seven volunteers from the community.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational report of that year rather than a specification. It records what was agreed, what was still open, and it notes that the IETF had no formal membership and no tradition of voting, so consensus was the only tool available.

today: RFC 1396 is an Informational RFC that specifies no standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the record of a working group that ran from August to December 1992 and reported on how the IETF and the IAB had decided to choose their own leaders and to handle standards actions. Its Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: Why the Standards Process Was in Dispute
sections.content:
The memo is a report written by Steve Crocker, who chaired the POISED working group, and he says at the outset that it necessarily represents his own perception, particularly of the period before the group existed. Quite a few people hold strong views about the overall sequence and about specific events, and his intent is to convey as neutral a point of view as possible.

The background is a technical worry that turned political. During 1991 there was great concern that the IP address space was being depleted and that the routing tables were growing too large. Some change to the IP addressing and routing mechanisms seemed inevitable, and it became urgent to explore what those changes should be. The ROAD working group was formed to study the issues and recommend changes. It returned with a specific recommendation for the short term but did not reach a conclusion on a long term plan.

The IESG then formulated a plan of action and forwarded its recommendations to the IAB. In June 1992, after the INET '92 meeting in Kobe, Japan, the IAB met and considered them. After doing so the IAB felt that additional ideas were also important, particularly some of the addressing ideas in the CLNP protocol, and communicated its concerns. There was immediate controversy along two dimensions. The technical question was what the best course was for evolving the IP protocol, and how important or useful the ideas in the OSI protocol stack were. The political question was who makes decisions within the Internet community, and who chooses who makes those decisions.

As often happens during periods of conflict, communication suffered. The June communication from the IAB was understood by many as an IAB decision, while many on the IAB felt they were opening up a discussion and that their memos were advice. Crocker attributes part of this miscommunication to the growing size of the technical community: when the community was much smaller the IAB was in close contact with the day-to-day workings of the technical groups, but with the creation of the IESG and the area directorates there are now two or three layers between a working group and the IAB.

The matter came to a head at the IETF meeting in July in Cambridge, Massachusetts, where it was made clear that the consideration of changes to the IP protocol remained open and that the decision process itself and the procedures for populating the IESG and IAB had to be examined. The procedures for selecting members had been derived from the creation of the Internet Society and its sponsorship of the IAB, developed in early 1992 and adopted by the Internet Society at its meeting in Kobe in June. In short, the Society was building the framework for supporting the community as fast as the community was questioning that framework.

After that meeting Vint Cerf, the Internet Society president, called for the formation of a working group to examine the processes, and especially the selection process. The group was formed during August, Crocker was asked to chair it, and a charter was written. The name is an accident: the acronym is due to Erik Huizer and originally stood for The Process for Organization of Internet Standards and Development, and it was shortened to fit the space available on paper and in the IETF Secretariat's database.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet was running out of addresses and its routing tables were growing, so the community had to decide what to do next. The board that oversees standards and the group that runs it sent different signals about who should decide, and the argument turned into a fight over authority. The result was a working group to look at how the process itself worked.

sections.title: Deliberations from August to Mid-November
sections.content:
The formation of the group gave the process issues a forum. An estimated 20 MB of messages filled up disks all over the world, and much of the discussion was fragmented or focused on narrow issues. The salient point that emerged was the need for a well defined process for selecting leaders, with explicit community representation in the selection process. There was also substantial discussion of the role of the IAB, to what extent it should make decisions and to what extent it should provide technical guidance, and of the relationship between the IAB and the IESG.

After several weeks of discussion Carl Malamud and Crocker attempted to capture the main elements of the discussion by presenting a specific proposal for the reorganization of the entire structure. Its main elements were: retention of the working group and area structure then in place within the IETF; replacement of the IAB and the IESG by two boards, one devoted to technical management and one devoted to oversight of the process; well defined terms for members of both boards; and selection by committees with input from the community.

Crocker notes that the proposal was technically radical in the sense that it proposed new structures to replace existing structures rather than changes within the existing system. It also focused all further discussion, and it set the stage for the fall IETF meeting in mid-November in Washington, D.C.
sections.plainLanguage: For three months the group argued by email. Two things came out of it: the need for a clear way of choosing the people who would run the standards process, with ordinary members represented in that choice, and the first draft of a proposal that would have replaced both the IAB and the IESG with two new boards.

sections.title: The November IETF Meeting and the New Decision Path
sections.content:
Because of the intensity of interest, POISED was one of the focal points of the November IETF meeting. The schedule included a plenary session on Tuesday morning to present the current state of the discussions, a formal POISED working group session on Tuesday afternoon, and an open IESG meeting on Thursday evening devoted to POISED issues. The formal schedule was only the tip of the iceberg: numerous meetings took place over breakfast, lunch and dinner, in the halls and off in the corners, and the more active participants probably had a dozen or more separate meetings over the three most active days, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

Progress happened at two key points. At the Tuesday afternoon working group meeting, Lyman Chapin, the IAB chair, Phill Gross, the IETF chair and an IAB member, and other IAB members proposed changes within the existing IAB and IESG structure which converged with the process management elements of the Malamud-Crocker proposal. The key point was that all processing of standards actions, including the final decision to advance a specification along the standards track, would be made by the IESG. Crocker notes that this change shortens the decision cycle and brings it a step closer to the working group, and that converging on it obviated the radical proposal and signalled the building of a consensus on how the standards process should evolve. Over the next two days attention turned to the selection process.

In contrast to the extraordinarily contentious open IESG meeting in Cambridge, the Thursday meeting was characterised by a strenuous effort by numerous people, representing diverse points of view, to reach consensus on the selection proposal, and it ended with a distinct decision to proceed on that basis. Given the consensus that emerged, the group decided to implement the selection process by the next IETF meeting, with the new IESG and IAB members beginning their terms at the end of the IETF meeting in March.

On the Friday, the IAB and the IESG met jointly to decide what to do next. Both groups agreed to implement the change in processing standards actions quickly and cooperatively, and to identify the positions that were open for selection. Within a couple of weeks the IAB had finished processing the standards actions in its queue, and the IESG began to handle standards actions on its own.
sections.plainLanguage: The meeting in Washington produced a bargain. The board would stop deciding things and would give that job to the group that handles the working groups, which shortens the path from a draft to a standard. The plan to replace both bodies was dropped, because the group could get what it wanted by changing the existing one.

sections.title: How the IAB and IESG Members Are Chosen
sections.content:
There was a strong feeling in the community that the IAB and IESG members should be selected with the consensus of the community. A natural mechanism for doing this would be formal voting, but Crocker points out that a formal voting process requires formal delineation of who is enfranchised. One of the strengths of the IETF, he writes, is that there is not any formal membership requirement, nor is there a tradition of decision through votes; decisions are generally reached by consensus with mediation by leaders when necessary.

The formula that emerged was that IAB and IESG members would be selected by a nomination and recruiting committee. The committee is to consist of seven members from the community, with non-voting representatives from the IAB and the IESG and a non-voting chair provided by the Internet Society. The seven members are volunteers, with selection by lot if there are more than seven volunteers. The only requirement for a volunteer is that they must have attended two IETF meetings, a requirement designed to ensure that the nomination committee has some familiarity with the Internet community and the standards process.

IAB and IESG members serve two years. Half of each body has terms starting in odd years and half in even years, so that half the membership turns over at a time. Selections to the IESG have to be ratified by the IAB, and selections to the IAB have to be ratified by the Internet Society. If the nomination committee cannot reach a consensus on a single candidate for each position, it may forward multiple nominations to the ratifying body, and the ratifying body selects the candidate.

A recall mechanism was outlined using a similar scheme. The Internet Society is to supply an ombudsman who will field complaints after all oversight processes have been exhausted. If the ombudsman cannot resolve a complaint after a cooling off period, a recall committee, selected at random among volunteering community members, will consider the matter, and a two thirds vote by that committee is necessary to remove someone.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no membership list to vote from, so the new rule avoids voting altogether. Seven volunteers who have been to two IETF meetings pick the candidates, and a second body signs off. Members serve two years, half at a time, and there is a way to remove someone who should not be there.

sections.title: The December Internet Society Meeting and What Was Next
sections.content:
The Internet Society Trustees met on December 10 and 11 at CNRI in Reston, Virginia. The process and organization of the IAB and the IETF was one of their major concerns. A session of the Trustees at 3:00 p.m. EST on December 10 was broadcast via the Internet; it was not clear how many people listened, but Geoff Huston, an Internet Trustee, was spliced in separately from Australia.

At that session Crocker presented the results of the POISED working group's deliberations and asked, on behalf of the IETF, that the Trustees approve the selection process described above. For the long run a new charter was needed, and given the compressed schedule for these activities there had been no time to draft and refine one, so the Trustees were asked to approve the general direction of the reorganization and to give temporary approval to the selection process so that the first round of selections could proceed.

The Trustees expressed strong approval for the work of the working group and general approval for the direction of the effort. One area of concern for the Trustees was the legal liability of the Internet Society regarding decisions the IESG might make in the future. They made it quite clear that they are not inclined to micromanage the IETF process, but that they do feel compelled to understand the legal issues and help construct a charter consistent with their responsibilities as Trustees. The session adjourned with agreement to proceed on the current course and for the IETF, the IAB and the Internet Society Trustees to work together to draft the appropriate charter.

The memo ends with what was still to do. Both the IESG and the IAB had selected the positions which must be filled through the new process, and Vint Cerf was working to find a chair for the nominations committee, with the process expected to move forward during January and February. Communications on the details of the nomination process were to be published on the IETF mailing list and possibly other forums, and the selection process was expected to be complete well before the next IETF meeting, preferably by the end of February. The other open item was the draft of a new charter for the IAB and the IETF and its adoption by the Internet Society, which Crocker describes as the next order of business for the working group.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Society's trustees, who were legally responsible for the organisation, approved the direction but wanted a proper charter written before the arrangement became permanent. They also wanted to be sure they understood their own legal position, since the group making the standards decisions would no longer be under their direct control.

sections.title: The Two Attachments
sections.content:
The first attachment is the message from Vint Cerf that started the working group, sent on 12 August 1992. It explains that in June 1992 the Internet Society Board of Trustees had received a proposed charter for an Internet Architecture Board to be created within the Society, to be made up of the then current members of the Internet Activities Board, with the functions of the IETF and the IRTF brought under the umbrella of the new board. The Trustees had voted to accept that charter, which is contained in RFC 1358.

The message then identifies three points as particularly important to consider: procedures for making appointments to the IAB; procedures for resolving disagreements among the IETF, the IESG and the IAB over matters pertaining to Internet standards; and methods for ensuring that for any particular Internet Standard the procedures have been followed satisfactorily by all parties, so that everyone with an interest has had a fair opportunity to be heard. Cerf asks the IETF to create a working group, with recommendations by the first of December 1992 so that they could be presented at the Trustees meeting scheduled for December 10. He notes that the current procedures for making IAB appointments are in the IAB charter, RFC 1358, and that RFC 1310 describes the current process by which Internet Standards are achieved.

The second attachment is the working group charter itself. The goal is to examine the Internet standards process and the responsibilities of the IAB, with attention to the relationship between the IAB and the IETF and IESG, and the three matters listed above are the ones the group will consider. It will begin with a review of the procedures for making IAB appointments as documented in RFC 1358 and of the standards-making process documented in RFC 1310.

The charter sets a goal of issuing a final report in time for IESG consideration and publication as an RFC before the Internet Society Board of Trustees meeting in December 1992, and notes that given the compressed timescale the group would conduct most of its deliberations by electronic mail on the POISED mailing list. There would also be a preliminary report and discussions at the November 1992 IETF meeting in Washington, D.C. The charter states that this will be a normal IETF working group, with the mailing list and all discussions completely open.

The milestones follow: in September 1992 gather the initial set of issues and write a preliminary report; in October post as an Internet Draft the initial recommendations to the Internet Society Board; in November open discussion and presentation of the work at the Washington, D.C. IETF meeting; in December submit the recommendations document to the IESG for posting as an Informational RFC, subsequently to be transmitted to the Internet Society Board. The memo's Security Considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in it.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo ends with the two documents that set the working group up: the email from the Internet Society president asking for it, and the charter that said what it should do and when. Both are included in full, so the reader can see the request and the answer.

viz.caption: THE RADICAL PROPOSAL AND WHAT WAS ADOPTED INSTEAD

left.title: The Malamud-Crocker proposal
left.desc: Replace the IAB and the IESG with two boards, one for technical management and one for process oversight, with well defined terms for their members.

right.title: What was adopted
right.desc: All processing of standards actions, including the final decision to advance a specification, is done by the IESG, inside the existing structure.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR CHOOSING THE PEOPLE WHO RUN THE STANDARDS PROCESS

items.title: Seven members
items.text: A nomination and recruiting committee of seven volunteers from the community, with non-voting representatives from the IAB and the IESG and a non-voting chair from the Internet Society.

items.title: Two meetings
items.text: The only requirement for a volunteer is that they have attended two IETF meetings.

items.title: Selection by lot
items.text: If more than seven people volunteer, the seven are chosen by lot.

items.title: Two-year terms
items.text: Members serve two years, with half of each body starting in odd years and half in even years.

items.title: Ratification
items.text: Selections to the IESG are ratified by the IAB; selections to the IAB are ratified by the Internet Society.

items.title: More than one candidate
items.text: If the committee cannot agree on a single candidate, it may forward several names and the ratifying body chooses.

items.title: Recall
items.text: An ombudsman hears complaints; if a complaint cannot be settled, a randomly chosen committee of volunteers may remove a member by a two thirds vote.
